thread.title: Apple Earnings: The Next IBM - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Hervé Blandin
title: Apple Earnings: The Next IBM - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) released the fiscal Q1 2019 results . As management revised the guidance at the beginning of January, the results didn't bring any surprise. The company's Q2 guidance and earnings call confirmed the contrast between the decline in revenue from the iPhone and the growth of its other businesses.
The company is now in the same situation as IBM Corp. ( IBM ). Its growth businesses (services, wearables, etc.) will have to compensate for the decline of the legacy high-margin business (iPhone).
The market values Apple at a modest price. But the growth businesses will have to offset the decline of revenue from the iPhone to justify a higher valuation.
Image source: Monoar via Pixabay
Q1 2019 earnings with no surprise Considering the revised guidance released at the beginning of the year, there was not much room left for surprises. The table below compares the reported fiscal Q1 results against the two previous outlooks.
Fiscal Q1 2019 guidance communicated during fiscal Q4 2018 Revised fiscal Q1 2019 guidance communicated on January, 2 Fiscal Q1 2019 results Revenue Between $89 billion and $93 billion Approximately $84 billion $84.3 billion Gross margin Between 38% and 38.5% Approximately 38% 38% Operating expenses Between $8.7 billion and $8.8 billion Approximately $8.7 billion $8.69 billion Other income/(expense) Approximately $300 million Approximately $550 million $560 million Tax rate Approximately 16.5% before discrete items Approximately 16.5% before discrete items 16.49% Source: Author, based on company reports
As expected, the iPhone and the Greater China area drove the 5% total revenue decline YoY.
Source: Q1 2019 financial statements
As shown below, some studies related to the Chinese market had also documented the decline of smartphone shipments before the earnings. The same study highlighted the impressive growing market share for Huawei.
Source: Canalys
Besides the weakness of the iPhone, Apple keeps on reporting record results for the other segments. For instance, Services revenue grew 19% YoY. Also, Wearables, Home and Accessories reached all-time highs, growing 33%.
The fiscal Q2 guidance shown below confirms this trend. During the earnings call, management said Q2 revenue from iPhone would drop, while other revenue would "grow nicely".
Guidance fiscal Q2 2019 Results fiscal Q2 2018 Revenue Between $55 billion and $59 billion $61.1 billion Gross margin Between 37 percent and 38 percent 38.3% Operating margin expense Between $8.5 billion and $8.6 billion $7.5 billion other income/(expense) $300 million $274 Tax rate 17% 14.5% Source: Author, based on company reports
A part of the anticipated decline in Q2 is due to the strong dollar that accounts for a difference of about $1.5 billion, according to management during the earnings call. But even if we adjust for this difference, the mid-point of the revenue guidance still represents a more than 4% decline compared with the reported revenue last year.
Is Apple the new IBM? If you are not familiar with IBM, the old tech company has been struggling over the past few years to keep revenue flat . But this revenue pattern hides the contrast between the decline of the legacy cash machine businesses and the growth of new activities .
The fiscal Q1 results and Q2 guidance show Apple is entering into the same revenue pattern as IBM . The iPhone is the declining cash cow business. In the meantime, Services and Wearables, Home and Accessories represent the growing segments.
As was the case with IBM a few years ago, the growth segments are not yet important enough to offset the legacy business decline. Revenue from the iPhone still exceeded $50 billion during Q1, while revenue from Services and Wearables, Home and Accessories stayed below $20 billion. And as it is the case with IBM, despite the revenue decline, the EPS is still growing, thanks to the share buyback program.
Of course, both companies operate in different businesses and address different markets (consumer vs. enterprise) . But in both cases, the investment thesis remains centered around the same question. Will the growth businesses succeed in replacing - or even exceeding - the declining cash machine ?
Since the revised revenue guidance, the valuation ratios of both companies have started to converge .
Data by YCharts
Some differences exist, though. With a net cash position at $130 billion, Apple has more flexibility in its capital allocation than IBM. The company still has the goal of reaching a neutral cash position, but Tim Cook said capital allocation would be discussed during the next earnings call. On the other hand, IBM will soon have to absorb the acquisition of Red Hat ( RHT ) and will have to focus on debt reduction.
From a business perspective, I prefer IBM. Apple is still dependent on the iPhone, which is more exposed to consumer trends. In fiscal Q1, iPhone sales still represented 61.7% of total revenue. And a part of Services is related to the iPhone.
Valuation linked to the declining iPhone revenue About the valuation, I still have the same opinion I expressed after the company's fiscal Q3 and Q4 2018 results.
Source: Author, based on company reports
With a P/E ratio TTM ex-cash at about 9, the valuation is low. But the dependency on the iPhone is a risky proposition. The decline of the iPhone is now a reality, and it is driving the total revenue decline.
Apple is still growing its EPS, though. But that is only thanks to the company's share buyback program. Q2 guidance shows that gross margin is expected to decrease, while operating expenses will grow YoY.
Conclusion Considering management had revised its guidance a few weeks before the earnings announcement, the fiscal Q1 results are not surprising . And the guidance for fiscal Q2 confirms that revenue decline from the iPhone was what was driving the total revenue decrease .
Apple is now entering into a new phase. Its cash cow business is diminishing, and the growing segments are not important enough to compensate for the loss of revenue .
The market values the company at a cheap price. But i nvesting in Apple is a bet on its capacity to grow the other segments to offset the declining revenue from the iPhone .
